name: Mask Your Intentions
description: Build attacks that share grips and starting movements so your next choice is harder to read. Use credible threats, controlled changes, and a clear positional fallback.
summary: An attack is harder to read when its early grips and movements also support another credible option.
overview: You do not need theatrical feints. Start by noticing the extra signal you give before a favorite move: a unique grip, a long pause, or a shift that serves only that attack.
key_takeaways: Use a setup that can lead to more than one action without dismantling your control.
Make the first threat useful on its own; if the opponent does not defend it, be prepared to continue.
Read a real change in their position before switching targets.
Conceal the choice of attack, not your partner’s chance to tap. Apply submissions with control.

bjj_applications.scenario: Your partner retreats their weight every time you prepare a butterfly sweep
bjj_applications.application: Begin your sweep setup from the same posture and grips you use to pull them forward or follow them as they retreat. Choose the action once their weight changes.
bjj_applications.outcome: The shared setup gives less advance notice of which direction you will use.

bjj_applications.scenario: A mounted opponent keeps both elbows close
bjj_applications.application: Develop a controlled collar-choke threat in the gi. If defending it moves an elbow away from the ribs, consider an arm attack only when your base and control support it; otherwise continue the choke setup or rebuild position.
bjj_applications.outcome: A second target can emerge from a genuine defense, without assuming the arm must become available.

bjj_applications.scenario: Your preferred passing side is obvious before you move
bjj_applications.application: Use a balanced stance and useful leg controls that allow an approach to either side. Change direction when their frames commit, keeping track of the returning knee.
bjj_applications.outcome: Your first grip no longer announces the entire pass.

common_mistakes.mistake: Faking an attack that cannot affect the opponent
common_mistakes.consequence: They have no reason to change their position.
common_mistakes.correction: Improve the first attack until it deserves a response.

common_mistakes.mistake: Switching because the combination says to, despite no opening
common_mistakes.consequence: You leave a workable attack for a second one with missing controls.
common_mistakes.correction: Continue the first threat or recover your position when the expected defense does not appear.

training_exercises.name: Same start, different choice
training_exercises.description: Pick two familiar actions from the same guard with overlapping grips. Show your partner the shared starting position, then let them defend freely. Choose from the actual response; reset on a sweep, pass, lost guard, or tap.
training_exercises.focus: Reduce unnecessary signals without losing a functional setup.

training_exercises.name: Find the tell
training_exercises.description: Record a short positional round with your partner’s agreement. Find the earliest moment they could identify your favorite attack, then repeat from that position with one unnecessary movement removed. Stop and reset after the attack or defense is resolved.
training_exercises.focus: Separate essential preparation from avoidable telegraphing.

knowledge_assessment.question: What should you do when the first attack is not defended?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Continue it if the controls are sound. The second attack is an option, not an obligation.
